This new “development” of old forms within a new consciousness—forms already superseded or dialectically overcome and preserved—is nothing other than the understanding of a particular age, or the understanding of its “appearance”: the understanding of the age itself as a phenomenon.

Hegel calls this fully developed self-understanding of an age its “science.” By this he means the knowledge that is “perfect” for its own time: the knowledge through which a particular age distinguishes itself from every other age, and through which it finally becomes fully conscious of itself—that is, genuinely human or historical, and therefore dialectical.

We can say that the Phenomenology describes only “sciences” of this kind. Or, to put it differently, it describes only the adequate self-understanding of historical ages, each corresponding to one of the fundamental theses, antitheses, or syntheses of the real dialectic.

It says nothing about the collapse of the old world in question, or about the preparation of the new world that follows it. Nor does it discuss the sudden revolutionary “birth” of that new world. It remains silent about the development of the new world itself, just as it remains silent about the different ways in which that world “appears” to the people living within it.

What it describes is only the “science” that this world eventually creates for itself. Such a science usually appears near the end of the world’s development, once that world has taken on its full form and become fully conscious of that form.
Then the Phenomenology jumps from one such “science” to another, leaving out everything that “happened” between them as well as everything that “happened” while each of them was coming into being.
But besides this phenomenologically justified fragmentation, there is another kind of omission that may seem even more outrageous to the reader—and to the critic.

The Phenomenology confines itself to “European” humanity and simply ignores the history of India, China, America, and so on. Strictly speaking, the phenomenologist studies only one line of historical development: a line traced by a single continuous historical tradition, or “memory” of the past. He says nothing about parallel processes that have no historical relation to one another—that is, processes that “know nothing” of one another.

This approach is perfectly justified insofar as the Phenomenology is the autobiography of its author and of his age. The phenomenologist is looking for his own “ancestors,” for the historical roots of his own age—for everything that is in some way present in himself and in that age, either as consciously remembered history or as an unconscious historical precondition.
From this point of view, a historical phenomenon such as pre-Columbian America naturally cannot concern him.

But insofar as the Phenomenology is also an anthropology—that is, a science of human beings in general—this exclusion can be justified only if all the possibilities of human existence have in fact been realized within “European” history, so that everything outside it is merely a repetition of something already found within it.
The Hegelian-Marxist philosophy of History takes precisely this view.

The dialectic described by Hegel is, in fact, only the dialectic of “European” humanity, and yet it is presented as the dialectic in general. In the same way, the Marxist dialectical laws governing real historical development were discovered entirely on the basis of “European” material, yet they are nevertheless applied to historical processes everywhere. This means that outside “Europe” there is supposedly nothing essentially new.

Of course, this claim would have to be proved by a proper concrete investigation, and there can be no question of undertaking one in our Phenomenology. The reader is therefore forced to accept this unstated claim on faith.
Even so, a few things can already be said in its favour.

There can be no doubt that the whole non-European world has, as it were, stopped in its independent historical development and is now falling under the influence of European culture. Non-European countries either remain frozen at a stage of historical development that Europe reached long ago and—whatever one may say—lead a rather impoverished and “sluggish” historical and cultural existence; or else, in “reviving” and beginning a new period of intense historical life, they introduce the “European order” into their own societies.

It is therefore more than likely that the future historical development of humanity will form a single unified process. All the more so because the existence of a World Union of Soviet Socialist Republics can already be regarded as fully assured.

As we know, a fundamental principle of the dialectic is that only one path can lead to a given point. So if the dialectic really exists—and if it does not, then the Phenomenology frankly makes no sense at all—the Phenomenology is perfectly entitled to restrict itself to the study of its “European” realization.

For if, in the future, the non-European world no longer differs from the European world, then this means that, in reality, it never differed from it in any essential respect before either, despite all the “external” and “contingent” differences that are the first things to catch the eye.
In any case, the Phenomenology contains a great many historical omissions and shortcuts. And this is all the more striking because, at the same time, it contains many repetitions.
Yet these repetitions are themselves phenomenologically justified. They too follow from the dialectical character of the object being described.

To begin with, the second part inevitably repeats what was already said in the first. The first part sets out the fundamental aspects and types of human existence, together with the general pattern of its historical development. The second part then describes the concrete realization of that pattern. So it is obvious that what first appeared in an abstract and general form will later return in a concrete form.
But there are also repetitions within the second part itself.
Precisely because it describes the phenomenological aspect of the real dialectic.

First, dialectical development continually “repeats,” so to speak, the same triadic pattern. There is always something common to every thesis, every antithesis, and every synthesis. So exactly the same observations may reappear at different stages of the description.

Second, the past is always “preserved” in the historical present—preserved, that is, through dialectical transformation. In this sense, the successive stages of development can be regarded as repeated versions of the same basic “appearance” on increasingly higher “levels.”

The phenomenologist will of course emphasize what is new at each stage. But if he described only the novelty, as though nothing else existed, he would badly distort the real appearance of the phenomenon. So in describing what is new, he is also forced to describe what is old within it—what was already there, and therefore what has already been described.

Certain repetitions are consequently unavoidable. They are necessary precisely because the description must bring out the dialectical character of the phenomenon—that is, the way earlier forms are preserved and transformed, and the way each new stage is mediated by what came before it.
Having dealt with these “omissions” and “shortcuts,” we still need to say a few words about the unusual “parallelism” of phenomenological description.

A phenomenological description, whether in the first or the second part, is divided into two main sections. One section, A, describes the “practical aspect of human existence.” The other, B, describes its “theoretical” aspect.
These descriptions are parallel in the sense that, although one is presented after the other, both concern the same appearance or dialectical process.

For example, desire, with which section A of the first part begins, and sensation, with which the corresponding section B begins, are not two independent “phenomena.” They are two aspects of one and the same thing. We can distinguish them artificially, but in reality they are inseparable and mutually complementary.
The “practical” aspect of the fundamental phenomena is described before the “theoretical” aspect only because human action is logically prior to human knowledge, even though the two are inseparable.

Exactly the same is true, and for the same reason, in the second part. There too the “theoretical” side of the dialectic of historical appearances is described after the “practical” side. But again, in reality the two exist at the same time and cannot actually be separated.

So, from the standpoint of the real historical process—and partly from the chronological standpoint as well—when the reader reaches the end of section A and begins section B, he must mentally return to the historical period whose appearance was described at the beginning of section A. From then on, each stage of one section corresponds to a stage in the other.
We therefore have two genuinely parallel phenomenological descriptions of one and the same process.
But we must not imagine that section A describes the real existence of the historical process itself.
Section A is just as phenomenological as section B. It too describes only the appearances of the real historical process, not the process itself.

A “cosmological”—and Marxist—description of History must likewise distinguish two parallel sections. One discusses the real historical processes, above all the economic ones. The other discusses the “ideological superstructures” in which those real processes are reflected within the corresponding consciousness.

The Phenomenology as a whole, by contrast, describes only the “ideological superstructures” of History, if one wants to put it that way. What distinguishes it from Cosmology is simply that it does not trace those superstructures back, as Cosmology does, to their real “causes”—that is, to the corresponding material foundations.

The Phenomenology deals with the “appearances” of the practical side of human or historical existence, not with that practical side itself. And the same is true of the theoretical side of human existence: the Phenomenology speaks only about its appearances.

Even if we remain entirely within the limits of phenomenological description, however, and do not refer the “appearance” back to the reality that appears, we can still distinguish two fundamental aspects within any given historical phenomenon—or, if you prefer, within the “ideology” that reflects a particular historical age: a “practical” side and a “theoretical” side.

In both cases we are dealing with “theories,” with contents of consciousness, not with reality itself or with actual action. But there really are “theories,” in the broad sense, or contents of consciousness—“ideologies”—that have a practical character and directly influence the course of events, so that they effectively participate in those events.
And conversely, there are purely “theoretical” theories or ideologies that do no more than reflect a given reality like a mirror and carefully keep themselves, as it were, outside that reality.
In this sense, dividing the phenomenological description into two parallel sections has an “objective” basis and can therefore be justified theoretically.

From a purely theoretical point of view, however, it would be more natural to describe the two sides of the same phenomenon one after the other, beginning with the “practical” side, rather than splitting the discussion into two separate sections. The present arrangement means that one and the same phenomenon is described in different places in the book.
The only real justification for this procedure is, so to speak, pedagogical.

It makes the exposition easier to understand because it brings out more clearly the dialectical connections between the different “appearances.” Those connections really do develop along two parallel lines, though of course the two are only different aspects of one and the same real process.

This also means that assigning a given “appearance” to one section or the other is determined by the dialectical relation that appearance has to the other “appearances” within the relevant section. It is not determined simply by the character of the appearance itself.

For that reason, the division of phenomena between sections A and B can often look arbitrary. It may seem that they could just as easily have been arranged differently: a phenomenon described as “practical” might have been treated as “theoretical,” and vice versa.
But this is only an appearance. And it confirms once again that isolated parts of the Phenomenology cannot be understood—or properly handled—apart from their relation to the whole.
Why, then, do the various “philosophies” occupy such a prominent place among the “theoretical” phenomena?
The answer becomes clear once we remember that the Phenomenology is not only an autobiography and an anthropology. It is also a dialectical—that is, historical—introduction to philosophy.

The Phenomenology must show how and why the dialectical development of the history of European philosophy ultimately led to the philosophy whose first, introductory part is the Phenomenology presented here.
And this means that it must describe all the major philosophies that preceded it.
But the importance given to philosophy can also be justified independently of this consideration.

An age usually achieves its fullest and most exact understanding of itself in the philosophical System that corresponds to it. Such a System is nothing other than the complete and accurate reflection of that age within the consciousness appropriate to it.
Here, however, the word “philosophy” must be understood in a broad sense.
The reader will therefore see that, in its choice of material, the Phenomenology differs not only from ordinary, non-Marxist History, but also from the usual, non-dialectical histories of philosophy.
As for the other structural features of the Phenomenology, the reader will see and understand them better in the course of reading the book itself.
I will end this already overlong introduction here.

Almost everything said in it will, in one form or another, be repeated in the Phenomenology itself. Strictly speaking, the reader could therefore skip the introduction altogether. It certainly should not be regarded as indispensable or necessary.

Still, it seems to me that what has been said here will make the Phenomenology easier to read and understand, while also helping the reader avoid a number of possible misunderstandings and objections.
The purpose of this introduction is therefore entirely pedagogical.

And if, after finishing the book, the reader finds that reading this introduction beforehand really did make the Phenomenology easier to understand, then the introduction—its length as well as its contents—will have been justified pedagogically.
It does not claim, however, to be fully “convincing.” Whatever is said here can be justified theoretically only insofar as it is also contained in the text of the Phenomenology itself.
As for truth in the full sense, it can ultimately be established only by the System as a whole.

1) The Greeks were entirely right to use the word logos—“discourse”—for reason, the principle that distinguishes human beings from animals. To counter certain mystical and Romantic tendencies, we should state this firmly: without discourse, there is nothing “rational,” and therefore nothing human.

By “discourse,” however, I do not mean separate vocal gestures of the kind we also find in animals, or even articulated combinations of sounds like the “words” and “sentences” spoken by parrots. I mean conversation in the proper sense: the ability to ask questions about any phenomenon whatsoever in the real world, and the ability to give some kind of answer to any such question. Descartes was right to emphasize that we cannot imagine this capacity in an animal, or even in the most perfect automaton. (See Descartes, Discourse on the Method, ed. Adam and Tannery, vol. VI [1902], p. 56 ff.)

2) The phrase “meaningful discourse” needs to be emphasized. As we will see later, it allows us to distinguish philosophy, on the one hand, from science—in the sense of knowledge of nature—and, on the other, from art and every form of “mysticism.”

As we will see, natural science finds its final expression not in discourse but in mathematical formulas, which cannot be translated into ordinary language. Science is therefore, by its very nature, unable to provide the answers philosophy seeks.

The same applies to art. Insofar as it expresses itself through non-discursive means—colors, sounds, and so on—it naturally has nothing in common with philosophy and contributes nothing to our becoming conscious of life.
Finally, the philosopher rejects all “mystical-magical” phenomena that replace meaningful discourse with rituals of one kind or another, or with silent “ecstasies.”
(The case of literature is more difficult. Literature does contain philosophical elements. I will discuss this later.)

3) At the beginning of pagan Greek—that is, “rational”—philosophy, we find the command adopted by Socrates and Plato: “Know yourself.” At the beginning of Christian—that is, “revealed”—pseudophilosophy, we find something similar in Augustine, who begins his philosophical reflections from the desire to know himself, or to know his “soul,” as he puts it.
Unlike Socrates and Plato, however, Augustine says from the outset that he wishes to know two things, and only two: his soul and god.

Yet Augustine himself adds that the question of god, when properly posed and clarified, does not arise from the question human beings ask about their own “soul.” It necessarily presupposes the “divine revelation” given in the Bible—that is, in the book supposedly dictated by god himself, including, in particular, the account of his creating the world by an act of will alone.

4) I add the qualification “strictly speaking” because, as we will see later, even after introducing the concept of “revelation”—which is obviously irrational—they still cannot, in principle, avoid logical contradictions between their own answers to questions about humanity and god. And contradiction rules out “rationality.”

5) The followers of “spiritualism,” for example, or the “Surrealists” who are fashionable in the West today, clearly rely on the concept of revelation insofar as they believe that ultimate truths are disclosed to human beings in sleep, under narcotics, through “automatic (unconscious) writing,” and so on. This does not prevent some of them from being militant atheists.
